1.pericope_label: Ephraim's quarrel with Jephthah; Shibboleth at the fords of Jordan

schools.summary: Put pride at the bottom of the quarrel, since only by pride comes contention, and proud men count all honours lost that go beside themselves. Note that Ephraim had picked the same fight with Gideon, who was of Manasseh on the west of Jordan as Jephthah was of Manasseh on the east, and that these two tribes, being nearest of kin as sons of Joseph, were more jealous of one another than any other pair -- Jacob having crossed his hands, Ephraim would not endure that Manasseh should have any honour in the meantime. It is a pity that kindred, which should be an inducement to peace, so often occasions strife; a brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city. Then judge the anger on two counts. It was causeless, since the men of Gilead and not of Ephraim had made him their captain, so he had no authority to summon them, and no harm was done though their hands were not employed. And it was outrageous: men who should have come to congratulate a conqueror, and to condole with a father bereaved of his only child, came instead to burn him in his house. Those resentments that have the least reason for them commonly have the most rage in them.

Give the tribe its settled character from the whole book: slothful and acquiescent in time of oppression, turbulently arrogant when others have taken the initiative and won the victory, so that they brought the humiliation on their own heads. The threat to burn a man alive in his house shows the wild manners of the age. Handle the disputed taunt honestly, admitting that translation and meaning are both uncertain: it may be a contemptuous disclaimer of kinship, calling the eastern Manassites a race of runaways belonging to neither tribe, or, as another has it, a mob of nameless men set between two illustrious tribes. Note the bitter retribution in the wording, since the phrase used of the fugitives at the fords is exactly the one Ephraim had used as a taunt. Say what the fords meant: cutting off escape was excusable against a foreign invader, but to leave no chance of flight to Israelites in a civil war showed terrible exasperation, and the question at the crossing was needed to distinguish fugitives from harmless travellers and merchants. On the test word, give its senses -- ford, depth of waters, channel -- and record that the Greek made it an ear of corn, while rejecting that as unsuitable here.

Read the summons as jealousy: they called each other to arms, fearing that Gilead should acquire too much power. Explain the phrase about putting one's life in one's hand from the gesture behind it, a man laying hold of his sword or bow, which is at once his sole defence and the very thing his enemy aims at, so that it is fight and conquer or die; the conqueror in the prophet who says his own arm brought him salvation confirms the sense. Where the meaning of a taunt cannot be recovered, say so plainly rather than inventing one. And on the test word, spend the labour where it is needed: against those who find the difference between the two letters imperceptible, insist that a Hebrew ear caught it at once, as a native Arabic speaker distinguishes two letters a European never hears; and argue it from the spelling itself, since the second letter would not have been written at all if there were nothing in the sound to mark.

Correct the number and the grammar together. The Hebrew has a man of Ephraim, meaning not one man but a body of them who met and joined as one; and their strength may be reckoned at no fewer than fifty thousand, since forty-two thousand fell. Show next what the answer establishes about the war: it had been a contention between the Gileadites and the Ammonites over territory, not a private quarrel of Jephthah's, and it concerned chiefly the two tribes and a half, who cannot be blamed for defending themselves alone if they could without drawing in the rest. Account for the Gileadites reaching the fords first, whether by being swifter of foot or by taking a nearer way, being better acquainted with their own country. And read the test word in its setting: it means the stream they were standing at, so that the demand was in effect to ask leave to cross, and men in a hurry and off their guard said it as they had always said it.

sides.position: Pride, since only by pride comes contention; the same tribe had quarrelled with Gideon on the same ground, and kinship between Ephraim and Manasseh had bred jealousy rather than peace
A settled character running through the whole book -- slothful under oppression, turbulently arrogant once others had won the victory
Jealousy lest Gilead should acquire too much power

debates.question: What does the taunt about fugitives of Ephraim mean?

sides.position: A contemptuous disclaimer of kinship: the eastern Manassites are runaways belonging to neither tribe, a taunt perhaps true enough of men who fled across the river in debt or disgrace
That the Gileadites are a mob of nameless men dwelling between two illustrious tribes
Where the point of the reproach lies cannot easily be ascertained

debates.question: What does the test word mean, and was the difference in sound real?

sides.position: A stream or flood -- and not an ear of corn, which is quite unsuitable here
Ford, depth of waters, channel; though the Greek version rendered it an ear of corn and one manuscript simply paraphrases it as the watchword
The stream they were then standing at, so the demand was in effect to ask leave to cross
The question that matters is the sound, and against those who find the two letters indistinguishable a Hebrew ear caught the difference at once, as the spelling itself proves

outliers.note: Alone draws the moral the test word has since acquired, that Shibboleth stands for the minute differences religious parties press to internecine ferocity, while carefully noting that here the defective pronunciation was not the reason for killing a man but only the sign that he was an Ephraimite.

Alone argues at length that the two Hebrew letters were genuinely distinguishable, against those who find the difference imperceptible, comparing two Arabic letters that a native tells apart instantly and a European seldom catches, and arguing from the spelling that the distinction must have been audible.

themes: the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together... we will burn thine house upon thee with fire
I and my people were at great strife with the children of Ammon; and when I called you, ye delivered me not
Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth; for he could not frame to pronounce it right

7.pericope_label: Jephthah dies; Ibzan, Elon and Abdon judge Israel

schools.summary: Admit how little the title tells us: the word marks a recognised judge, but nothing shows the limits of jurisdiction or the amount of authority the office carried. What can be inferred is that the formula makes these men successors of Jephthah one after another, so their rule extended over the tribes east of Jordan and perhaps the northern ones west of it. On the burial place press the textual point, since the grave of so renowned a man was not likely to be forgotten: the Hebrew says only in cities of Gilead, and a single altered letter yields the reading of the Greek and Latin versions, in his own city. Decide the Bethlehem question against the southern town, giving both reasons -- that this book itself distinguishes the other as Bethlehem Judah, and that Judah at this period stood aloof from the general life of the nation -- and note that the next judge was a Zebulonite. Reject the identification of Ibzan with Boaz as having nothing to support it. Then work the names: one judge is called a terebinth and buried in a place whose identical letters with other vowels mean a gazelle; another is called servant, and his father bears a name afterwards famous in Jewish learning. Correct the English where it has aged, since sons of sons means grandsons and not nephews; and locate the burial sites on the ground.

Account for the shortness of the six years rather than passing over it: after the affair of the Ephraimites he was acknowledged by all Israel, but did not live long, being perhaps depressed and worn away with grief on his daughter's account and by the other troubles that attended him. On the next judge, report the tradition fairly -- that there were two towns of the name, that Josephus places him in Judah, and that because Boaz was of that place and lived in the days of the judges the Jewish teachers have thought them the same man. Then take the sixty children and make the comparison the text invites. It is uncommon enough for one man to have so many, and rarer still for the sexes to be equal; and the contrast with the judge before him is sharp, who had one daughter, an only child, and she by reason of his vow not suffered to marry. Such a difference God in his all-wise providence makes even among good men, and a numerous family is no certain characteristic of one.

Add up what these brief notices amount to. Six years, then seven, then ten, then eight: thirty-one years in all during which Israel had peace in all their borders, and it was in that time of rest that they corrupted themselves and were afterwards delivered into the hand of the Philistines. Translate the marks of state into terms a reader will feel -- riding fine asses then was no less dignified than riding in coaches now, so that these families all kept their carriages. Then say honestly what is missing. Nothing whatever is recorded of the civil administration of these judges, whether it was good or bad, and nothing of the state of religion under them; it is likely they enjoyed peace abroad and were able to prevent discord at home. Yet doubtless God was at work among them, though there were none to record the operations either of his hand or his Spirit, and the people who feared him no doubt bore testimony to the word of his grace.

Set the run of short judgeships under the proverb that fits it, that for the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof, many in a short time and successively, good men being removed at the beginning of their usefulness and about the time they have applied themselves to their business. Take the first of them for Bethlehem of Judah, David's city, and draw the consequence: that town was of old famous for increase, and was the very place where he should be born whose spiritual seed is to be as the stars of heaven. Observe that the number of his children and his own disposing of them all in marriage show he lived long, and that the great increase of his family and the alliances he made, added to his personal merit, may have helped fit him to be Israel's judge. And note the equal number of each sex, which does not often happen in one family, though in the great family of mankind he who at first made two, male and female, preserves by his wise providence a succession of both in some sort of equality.

debates.question: Which Bethlehem did Ibzan come from?

sides.position: Bethlehem of Judah, David's city, and the place where he should be born whose spiritual seed is as the stars
Judah, on the authority of Josephus; and the Jewish teachers identify Ibzan with Boaz, who was of that town and lived in the days of the judges

Not Judah. This book itself distinguishes the southern town as Bethlehem Judah, and Judah stood aloof from the national life at this period; the Bethlehem in Zebulun is likelier, since the next judge was a Zebulonite. The identification with Boaz has nothing to support it
Hardly the town in Judah, despite Josephus; probably the one in Zebulun

debates.question: What is to be made of the silence about these judges?

sides.position: They cover thirty-one years of peace in which Israel corrupted itself; nothing is recorded of their administration or of religion under them, yet God was doubtless at work with none to record it
The formula shows only that they succeeded one another, so their rule extended over the eastern tribes and perhaps the northern ones; nothing shows the limits of a judge's jurisdiction or authority
For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof, good men being removed at the beginning of their usefulness

outliers.note: Alone works these verses almost entirely through names, deriving one judge's name from the terebinth and noting that easterners are still named from trees, finding a play of words between that name and his burial place, which with other vowels means a gazelle, and observing that the father of the last judge bears a name afterwards famous in Jewish learning.

Alone totals the thirty-one years these judgeships covered and says plainly what is missing from them, that nothing is recorded of the civil administration, whether good or bad, nor of the state of religion, yet that God was doubtless at work among them though there were none to record the operations of his hand or his Spirit.

themes: And Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then died Jephthah the Gileadite
he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, whom he sent abroad
he had forty sons and thirty nephews, that rode on threescore and ten ass colts
